title: EU Leaders Fail to Agree 2028–2034 Budget as Ukraine Loan Talks Stall
summary: European Union leaders ended a special summit in Brussels on Thursday without agreement on the bloc's 2028–2034 budget, after more than 12 hours of talks. European Council President António Costa told reporters early on Friday: "We didn't reach an agreement." Leaders were split over the size of the nearly €1.6 trillion spending plan, with some states pushing for deeper cuts while most opposed them and defended farm and regional funding. A proposed €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027 also remains undecided, though 24 of the 27 member states back it; the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia do not, and Bulgaria would take part only in the non-military portion. Leaders will try again at a summit on December 17–18, with Costa insisting a deal must be reached by the end of the year so the budget can take effect on January 1, 2028.
why: The failure leaves both the EU's seven-year spending plans and a key source of funding for Ukraine in limbo — and with elections across Europe in 2027, agreement could get even harder if no deal is struck in December.

title: Two Italians Killed in Drone Attack on Kuwait Air Defence Site as Iran Denies Role
summary: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia were killed on Thursday in a drone attack on an air defence surveillance station in Kuwait. Kuwait's defence ministry said the men were wounded by falling shrapnel after a number of drones were detected and intercepted at what it called a vital facility, and later died of their injuries; a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were also wounded. Italy and Kuwait blame Iran for the attack, while Tehran denies any involvement — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the incident suspicious and said Iran was ready to work with Kuwait and Italy to determine its cause. Italy's foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, told the Senate in Rome that Italy would lodge a formal complaint with the Iranian embassy.
why: The attack shows the regional war that began in late February spreading to Gulf states and drawing in European nationals, raising pressure on Rome and Berlin and the risk of a wider confrontation — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU must step up pressure on Iran.

title: Israel Threatens to Displace One Million Gazans Unless Hamas Disarms
summary: Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz warned on Thursday that Hamas must disarm voluntarily under US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, or the Israeli military will disarm it by force in a new offensive, Operation Gideon's Chariots II. Katz said the operation would include another evacuation of one million Gaza residents southward, and claimed 70 per cent of Gaza's territory has been destroyed and is under Israeli military control. Hamas announced in July 2026 that it had agreed to hand over its weapons to a Palestinian technocratic committee under Trump's Board of Peace, but has not disarmed, while Israel has refused to begin withdrawing its forces. The threat comes as Israeli forces continue targeted killings in Gaza despite the ceasefire that took effect in October 2025.
why: The threat puts the fragile Gaza ceasefire at risk of collapse: a renewed offensive displacing a million people would be the largest forced movement in Gaza since the war began, and the two sides remain deadlocked on disarmament and withdrawal.

title: US Proposes New Tariffs on 14 Trading Partners Over Excess Factory Capacity
summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, after an eight-month Section 301 investigation into what it calls structural excess industrial capacity. China would face the highest rate — a proposed 20% on top of roughly 25% in duties from President Trump's first term, rising to 40% if the current US-China trade truce breaks down — while the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan would face a 15% rate within agreed trade-deal caps. The duties will go through a public comment period and hearings before taking effect, with implementation expected in January 2027 at the earliest. Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals for now, and both China and the European Commission have rejected the overcapacity accusations.
why: The proposal would hit nearly all of America's biggest trading partners at once and rebuilds the tariff programme the Supreme Court struck down in February on a new legal footing — a move that could reshape global trade costs and supply chains in 2027.

title: Pakistan's First Astronaut Boards China's Space Station on Shenzhou-24
summary: China launched the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft on Wednesday, carrying Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to the Tiangong space station — the first foreign astronaut ever to board it, and the first Pakistani to reach orbit. Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan Air Force pilot flying as a payload specialist, launched alongside commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, and the spacecraft docked with Tiangong about three and a half hours later. Ali will spend about a week aboard the station conducting experiments, including one on photosynthetic cyanobacteria, before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. The mission is the first joint crewed flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in China's space programme, following a February 2025 agreement between Beijing and Islamabad.
why: Tiangong has been a Chinese-only station since it became fully operational in 2022, so opening it to a foreign crew member marks a new phase in China's space diplomacy — and makes Pakistan the latest country to join human spaceflight.

title: Leaked Russian Statistics Put War Dead in Ukraine at Nearly 500,000
summary: At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, according to leaked death records from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat, analysed by the BBC. The records — more than 11 million death registrations from 2021 to September 2026, obtained in a hack by the Belarusian group Cyber Partisans and Ukraine's Silent Crow — were cross-checked against the BBC and Mediazona's named list of confirmed deaths, matching 90% of the records. Rosstat admitted a cyber-attack but denied any protected data had leaked, and Moscow has not published an official death toll since September 2022, when it last named 5,937 dead. Meduza and Mediazona, analysing the same files, estimate the true toll exceeds 720,000 once soldiers still listed as missing are included.
why: The leak gives the first data-based picture of the war's human cost drawn from Russia's own records — far above anything Moscow has acknowledged — and it shows the war has become the leading cause of death for young Russian men, reshaping how the conflict's scale is understood worldwide.

title: Solomon Islands Signs Security Treaty With Australia, Ruling Out Any Foreign Military Base
summary: The Solomon Islands signed a security treaty with Australia on Wednesday in Canberra, naming Australia its primary security partner and declaring it will never allow a foreign military base on its soil. Prime Ministers Matthew Wale and Anthony Albanese signed the pact days after reports that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew its controversial 2022 security deal with China, which is due to expire in early 2027; Wale declined to confirm or deny those reports, citing a non-disclosure clause in the China treaty. The wide-ranging treaty also covers Australian investment in infrastructure, education and renewable energy, improved visa arrangements for Solomon Islanders, and consultation with Canberra on critical infrastructure.
why: The Solomon Islands sits on the sea route between the United States and Australia, so the treaty closes off a feared Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific and marks a major shift in the contest for influence between China and US allies in the region.

title: Houthis Claim Strikes on Saudi Arabia's Largest Oil Refinery and Riyadh Financial District
summary: Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom's largest, saying the strike caused fires, and that they had also attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura, without confirming the refinery itself was hit, while satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showed thick black smoke around the refinery and NASA fire-detection data confirmed brightly burning heat sources nearby. The claims followed a Houthi drone strike on Tuesday on a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District that wounded 11 people, and a Saudi retaliatory strike overnight on the Houthi-held port of Hodeidah.
why: Ras Tanura sits beside one of the world's biggest crude export terminals, so attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and the capital's financial district raise the risk to global energy supplies — and show the US-Iran war's spillover widening across the region.

title: Iran Claims More Tankers Hit Mines in Strait of Hormuz as It Tightens Its Grip
summary: Iran's navy said on Tuesday that two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the Revolutionary Guard claimed three tankers had hit mines despite a US Navy escort. Iran's army chief said the waterway would be "more closed day by day," and the navy said the strait "will never open until Iran's goals and demands are met." Neither claim has been independently verified — no ships were named and no casualty figures were given — while the UK maritime agency UKMTO separately confirmed three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles while transiting eastbound on Sunday.
why: The Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil, so disputed claims of mines and attacks on tankers raise the risk to global energy supplies — and of a wider confrontation between Iran and the United States.

title: World Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya
summary: On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2016-2017 "clearance operations." It is the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has found a state responsible for genocide. The court found Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of civilians, committed widespread sexual violence and destroyed Rohingya villages, concluding the only reasonable inference was an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population. Myanmar was ordered to pay reparations, investigate and prosecute those responsible, and allow the safe, voluntary return of the more than 700,000 Rohingya who fled to Bangladesh.
why: The ruling sets a historic precedent in international law — the first time the world's highest court has held a state guilty of genocide — and gives the displaced Rohingya a formal legal basis to demand justice and return home, though enforcement now rests with the international community.

title: Ukraine Sinks Russian Warship in Libya, Taking Its Drone War to the Mediterranean
summary: Ukraine said on Monday that its naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, in Kyiv’s first acknowledged attack in the country. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones were used in the operation, which also destroyed a Ka-27 combat helicopter aboard the ship and hit the Russian cargo vessel MV Angara, which Kyiv says Moscow used to transport weapons. Satellite imagery showed the corvette capsized and largely submerged after the strike. Libya’s eastern-based government said the ship had docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement with Russia and has asked the United Nations to investigate, while the Tripoli government objected to Libya being drawn into external conflicts.
why: The strike carries the Russia-Ukraine war into the Mediterranean, showing Kyiv can hit Russian military logistics far beyond the Black Sea — and dragging a divided Libya deeper into a conflict it did not choose.

sources.name: Associated Press via NPR / North Country Public Radio

summary: Nearly 200 countries closed the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday without an overarching agreement, after negotiations ran two days overtime and became the longest UN climate conference in history. The European Union, Pacific island nations and other delegations rejected the final draft because it did not directly mention fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming, while oil-producing states led by Saudi Arabia had pushed to keep that language out. Rows over climate finance for poorer countries deepened the deadlock, and the summit also marked a formal acknowledgement that the world is set to overshoot the 1.5C warming limit agreed in Paris.
title: COP31 Climate Talks End Without a Deal Over Fossil Fuels
why: Without a shared deal naming fossil fuels or unlocking fresh finance, the global effort to slow warming and help vulnerable countries adapt heads into next year's talks with no new momentum.

title: NATO Vows to Defend Space After Reports Russia May Launch Nuclear-Armed Satellite
summary: German public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported on Monday that Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead, dubbed “Sputnik-S”, within 60 days — possibly before the end of the year. The satellite has reportedly been assembled and stored near Moscow for several years, and an intelligence assessment shared among NATO countries this month warned of a possible launch. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in Berlin that the alliance would defend against any threat in space, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz neither confirmed nor denied the reports but said they “reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue.” Moscow rejected the reports as propaganda, and placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would breach the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which Russia signed.
why: A nuclear detonation in orbit could destroy or disable large numbers of satellites and cripple communications and power grids on Earth with its electromagnetic pulse — which is why the European Space Agency’s chief called nuclear weapons in space “the ultimate nightmare scenario.”

title: Huawei Convicted on 10 of 12 Counts in US Criminal Trial Over Iran Business and Trade Secrets
summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei on Tuesday of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from American companies. Prosecutors said the company misled banks about its business in Iran and took technology from rivals including Cisco and T-Mobile over two decades. The jury acquitted Huawei of the two most sweeping charges — racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice — and the company said it expects to appeal. Sentencing is set for September 14, 2027.
why: The verdict closes an eight-year US prosecution of one of China's biggest technology companies and sets a precedent for how American courts treat foreign corporations accused of sanctions evasion and trade-secret theft — while the acquittal on the racketeering charge limits the penalties Huawei faces.

title: Judges Urge Prosecutors to Drop Bribery Charge in Netanyahu Corruption Trial
summary: Judges at the Jerusalem District Court on Wednesday recommended that prosecutors drop the bribery charge against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the case known as Case 4000, reconsider the charge in Case 2000, and seek a deal in the gifts case, Case 1000. Presiding Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman said the bribery charge presents considerable difficulties and the chances of conviction are low; the recommendation is not a ruling on the case. Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, and his trial began in 2020; he denies the charges. In Case 4000, prosecutors allege he granted regulatory favours worth around 1.8 billion shekels, about $500 million, to Bezeq Telecom in exchange for favourable coverage for himself and his wife on the Walla news site. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said she would review the court's comments with the prosecution, while Netanyahu called the recommendation a ray of light for truth and justice.
why: The judges' recommendation is a major boost for Israel's longest-serving prime minister and could end the most serious charge in a trial that has shadowed Israeli politics for years — though prosecutors may still press ahead, and the recommendation is not a ruling.
